items.title: Marty Sheller interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 9, 2022
items.q: And there were stories about how Marlon Brando used to hang out there.

ctx.x: Oh, right away I could pick out, I loved watching the dancers, then you can pick out — the more I learned about the music, the more I recognized what made a good dancer. And there were some that were obviously really sharp and that was a pleasure. I had the pleasure of playing at the Palladium many times and the dancers were terrific. And it’s inspiring to be on the bandstand here with the band that’s swinging, and the music is,

everybody feels it. You know how that is? Even though people don’t know what it is, they feel it. They know that something’s going on. They may not know what it is but they’re aware that something is going on. And the dancers would respond. The best dancers were the ones who were listening to the rhythms and would respond. Because there’s a history of African music where there were just drums and dancers. And that was carried on to Cuba and from Cuba to the United States. And there were some terrific dancers. As…

Was it odd, later on, when a group like Mongo Santamaria, Tito Puente, if you put that group in Town Hall, at a sit down concert, did it change the music because there was no room for dancing? Now the audience is sitting and listening.
